clips.title: What's inside|the *Great Pyramid*?
clips.yt_title: Muons found a hidden void above the Great Pyramid's Grand Gallery
clips.claim: Is there a hidden space inside the Great Pyramid, above its Grand Gallery?
clips.verdict_from: A void above the Grand Gallery: strong evidence.
clips.summary: Cosmic rays make muons, and empty space inside stone lets more of them through. In 2017, three kinds of detector saw extra muons from a space above the Great Pyramid's Grand Gallery, at least thirty metres long. A smaller corridor found the same way was later seen by a camera, but the Big Void has not had its camera yet.

clips.title: What really fell|at *Roswell*?
clips.yt_title: Roswell, 1947: the secret balloon project behind the flying saucer story
clips.claim: Was the debris behind the 1947 Roswell flying saucer story from a secret balloon project?
clips.verdict_from: Roswell's secret balloon: strong evidence.
clips.summary: In July 1947, the army air base at Roswell told the press it had captured a flying saucer; that evening, a general showed reporters a weather balloon. In 1994 the Air Force named a real secret, Project Mogul: balloon trains with reflectors from a toy company, sealed with tape printed with flowers. But the story kept changing, and no record says who destroyed the base's files.

clips.title: Can radar see|*648 metres* down?
clips.yt_title: Shafts 648 metres under Khafre's pyramid? The satellite radar claim, weighed
clips.claim: Did satellite radar find shafts and pillars reaching 648 metres under Khafre's pyramid?
clips.verdict_from: Shafts and pillars under Khafre: awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: In 2025, two researchers in Italy said satellite radar, read through the ground's faint trembling, had found eight shafts and two giant cubes down to 648 metres under Khafre's pyramid. Their idea is clever, but field checks of radar from space reach one or two metres, and there is no peer-reviewed paper yet. Bold ideas deserve a test, and this one could have one.

clips.title: Were some UFOs|*spy planes*?
clips.yt_title: Spy planes behind UFO sightings, and psychic spies: what the files admit
clips.claim: Were secret spy planes behind many of the UFO sightings of the late 1950s and 1960s?
clips.verdict_from: Spy planes behind the sightings: established.
clips.summary: From 1955, the secret U-2 spy plane flew far above the airliners of the day, its silver wings catching the sun at sunrise and sunset. Officials at the CIA later estimated that over half of UFO reports from the late 1950s through the 1960s were spy flights. Agencies also paid people to spy with their minds for twenty-three years, and that paperwork surfaced in the end too.

clips.title: A stone door|with *copper pins*?
clips.yt_title: Robots found stone doors with copper pins inside the Great Pyramid's shafts
clips.claim: Are there small stone doors, with copper pins, inside the Great Pyramid's narrow shafts?
clips.verdict_from: Stone doors in the Queen's Chamber shafts: established; what lies beyond them, an open question.
clips.summary: Two shafts about twenty centimetres square climb from the Queen's Chamber in the Great Pyramid. In 1993 a robot found a small stone door with two copper pins more than sixty metres in, and later robots looked past it to another stone, red paint marks and a looped pin, all shown in public. What lies past the last stone, nobody yet knows.

clips.title: How fast was|the *Navy's UFO*?
clips.yt_title: The Navy's Go Fast video: was the object just drifting with the wind?
clips.claim: Was the object in the Navy's Go Fast video just drifting with the wind?
clips.verdict_from: Go Fast drifting with the wind: plausible.
clips.summary: In 2017, the New York Times revealed a secret Pentagon UFO study, along with three Navy infrared videos. From the camera's own readings, NASA's independent panel put the Go Fast object about four thousand metres up, at roughly sixty-five kilometres an hour: a typical wind at that height. The Tic Tac, seen by four aviators, still has no published official explanation.

clips.title: Was the Sphinx|worn by *rain*?
clips.yt_title: Was the Great Sphinx worn by rain, thousands of years before Khafre?
clips.claim: Does rain erosion mean the Great Sphinx is thousands of years older than Khafre?
clips.verdict_from: A Sphinx thousands of years older than Khafre: awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: The pit walls around the Great Sphinx are deeply worn, and in 1992 the geologist Robert Schoch read that as rain, dating the first carving to between seven thousand and five thousand BCE. Others point to salt and underground water, and the temple built from the pit's blocks looks like one project with the Sphinx, under Khafre. The wear is real, but weathering is a poor clock.

clips.title: Did America hide|*crashed craft*?
clips.yt_title: Crashed craft and non-human bodies? The 2023 testimony to Congress, weighed
clips.claim: Has America secretly recovered crashed craft, and bodies, of non-human origin?
clips.verdict_from: Crashed craft and bodies, from Roswell to the hearing room: awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: In July 2023, former intelligence officer David Grusch told Congress under oath that America had recovered crashed craft and non-human bodies, as others had told him. NASA's panel and the Pentagon found no evidence of alien technology, and the 2026 file releases held no craft, bodies or material. One piece of material, examined in public by independent labs, would change that.

clips.title: Who first|told of *Atlantis*?
clips.yt_title: Atlantis has one ancient witness: Plato, writing around 360 BCE
clips.claim: Is Plato, writing around 360 BCE, the only ancient source for the story of Atlantis?
clips.verdict_from: Established: Plato wrote the story around 360 BCE, and his is the only ancient source.
clips.summary: Around 360 BCE, Plato wrote of Atlantis in two dialogues, the Timaeus and the Critias, as a tale passed from Egyptian priests to Solon and down a family. In the story, Atlantis is the proud sea power set against an ideal Athens. No older text has been found, and the Critias breaks off mid-sentence: our only witness is a brilliant storyteller.

clips.title: A *spaceman* in|Sahara rock art?
clips.yt_title: The great Martian god of Tassili: a spaceman, or a way of painting?
clips.claim: Do the round-headed giants painted at Tassili n'Ajjer show visitors in space helmets?
clips.verdict_from: Spacemen in the Tassili paintings: ruled out.
clips.summary: In 1956, the explorer Henri Lhote met a painted giant with a smooth, blank head in a rock shelter in south-east Algeria, and nicknamed it the great Martian god, half in jest, it seems. These Round Head figures date to about nine and a half to seven and a half thousand years ago, and look like a way of painting. Sponged for brighter copies, they faded faster.

clips.chapter: A date at the end of the ice
clips.title: Plato's date,|an *Ice Age* clue?
clips.yt_title: Plato's Atlantis date and the end of the Ice Age: clue or coincidence?
clips.claim: Is it more than coincidence that Plato's date for Atlantis falls at the end of the Ice Age?
clips.verdict_from: Plato's date beside the end of the ice is a coincidence worth noticing: a clue to check, not an answer.
clips.summary: Plato's story sets Atlantis about 9600 BCE, and Greenland's ice dates the end of the last Ice Age cold snap to about 9700 BCE, give or take a century. Seas were rising then and drowning coasts where people lived, but people worked stone, not metal. The rising sea is real; the triremes in Atlantis's docks are the warships of Plato's own day.

clips.title: A light bulb|and a *rocket*?
clips.yt_title: A light bulb at Dendera and a rocket at Palenque? Read the captions
clips.claim: Do the Dendera bulb carving and Pakal's tomb lid show an electric lamp and a rocket?
clips.verdict_from: An electric lamp at Dendera: ruled out. A rocket on Pakal's lid: ruled out.
clips.summary: In a crypt at Dendera, in Egypt, a carving looks like a giant bulb, but its hieroglyphs name a snake god rising from a lotus, and give its material: gold. At Palenque, in Mexico, the lid seen as a rocket names King Pakal, who died in 683, and shows the Maya World Tree. Experts still debate whether the king is falling into the underworld or rising reborn.

clips.chapter: No room on the sea floor
clips.title: Is Atlantis under|the *Atlantic*?
clips.yt_title: Is Atlantis under the Atlantic? What the sea floor and Spartel Bank show
clips.claim: Could a sunken continent, Atlantis, lie on the Atlantic floor beyond Gibraltar?
clips.verdict_from: A real island empire beyond Gibraltar, sunk in a day and a night around 9600 BCE? Ruled out.
clips.summary: In 1882, Ignatius Donnelly read the great ridge down the Atlantic as the drowned spine of Atlantis, not a silly guess then. Sound maps and drilling show the ridge is where new sea floor is born, and light continental rock does not sink. Spartel Bank, a small drowned island outside the Strait of Gibraltar, would probably have held simple fishermen, not an empire.

clips.title: Nazca lines:|*alien runways*?
clips.yt_title: Were the Nazca lines runways? How people drew giant figures in the desert
clips.claim: Were some of the Nazca lines in Peru made as runways for visitors from the sky?
clips.verdict_from: Runways at Nazca: ruled out; what the lines were for, an open question.
clips.summary: The Nazca figures in southern Peru were made by moving dark, rust-coated stones aside to show the pale ground beneath, which is far too soft for a runway. In 1982, Joe Nickell and five relatives used stakes and cord to plot a condor a hundred and thirty-four metres long in a Kentucky field, and from the air it matched. What the giant lines were for is still argued.

clips.title: Sahara, Bimini|or *Santorini*?
clips.yt_title: The Eye of the Sahara, Bimini and Santorini: was any of them Atlantis?
clips.claim: Was Plato's Atlantis the Eye of the Sahara, the stones off Bimini, or the island of Thera?
clips.verdict_from: And the Eye, the Bimini stones and Spartel Bank, as Plato's city? Natural, too young, or too small.
clips.summary: The Eye of the Sahara, rings of rock forty kilometres across, is eight times too big and far from the sea; the squared stones off Bimini are beachrock, with shells about three and a half thousand years old. Thera, today's Santorini, erupted around 1600 BCE, but Plato puts Atlantis beyond the Pillars of Heracles. Thera was a real catastrophe, and perhaps a distant memory.

clips.title: Did the ancients|use *batteries*?
clips.yt_title: Klerksdorp spheres and the Baghdad battery: lost technology, weighed
clips.claim: Was the clay jar found near Baghdad in 1936 a working battery in its own time?
clips.verdict_from: And the Baghdad jar as a working battery: awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: The grooved Klerksdorp spheres from South African mines are concretions, geologists say, and a steel blade scratches them. The clay jar found near Baghdad in 1936 holds a copper tube and an iron rod, and replicas filled with lemon juice give about half a volt. But no wires were found with it, and similar jars held rolls of papyrus: perhaps a holder for a blessing.

clips.title: Did a real city|*sink* in a night?
clips.yt_title: Helike: the real city of Poseidon that sank in one night in Plato's lifetime
clips.claim: Did Helike, a real city of Poseidon, sink into the sea in a single night in Plato's lifetime?
clips.verdict_from: Established too: ... Helike sank in 373 BCE
clips.summary: In the winter of 373 BCE, an earthquake by night and then the sea took Helike, a city famous for its temple of Poseidon, less than a hundred and fifty kilometres from Athens. Ninety-nine boreholes later found its ruins some three metres down, under what is dry land today. About a dozen years later, Plato wrote Atlantis; whether Helike shaped it, we can't know.

clips.title: Giant stones|*older* than Rome?
clips.yt_title: Are Baalbek's giant blocks older than Rome? How you date a wall
clips.claim: Are the giant lower courses at Baalbek older than the Roman temple built on top of them?
clips.verdict_from: Baalbek's giants older than Rome: awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: At Baalbek in Lebanon, a Roman temple to Jupiter sits on a platform holding three limestone blocks about nineteen metres long, and the writer Graham Hancock fairly asks if they are older than Rome. The giant platform wraps around an older, smaller one, and quarry pottery dates to early Roman times. The test is a sealed layer under the trilithon.

clips.title: Who carved giants|*without* metal?
clips.yt_title: How hunters carved Göbekli Tepe's stone giants without metal
clips.claim: Did people raise Göbekli Tepe's stone giants without metal, pottery or farm animals?
clips.verdict_from: Established: from about nine and a half thousand BCE, people here raised stone giants, without pottery, metal or farm animals.
clips.summary: On a ridge in southeast Turkey, round enclosures hold T-shaped stone pillars with carved arms, hands and belts: giants in stone. They were cut in the quarry next door with flint picks, by people who ate gazelle and wild cattle: animals hunted, not herded. The textbooks said farming first, then monuments; here the giants came first.

clips.title: How do you move|*1,000 tonnes*?
clips.yt_title: How do you move a 1,000-tonne stone? Sledges, wet sand, capstans and rope
clips.claim: Did moving stones of a thousand tonnes need a lost high technology?
clips.verdict_from: A lost high technology, needed to move these stones: ruled out.
clips.summary: The enemy is friction, not weight: an Egyptian tomb scene shows a statue of about sixty tonnes on a sledge as a man pours water on the sand, and in 2014 physicists found the right amount of water cuts the pull by about half. In 1770, about four hundred people in Russia hauled a granite boulder of more than a thousand tonnes. How Baalbek's giants were raised is still unknown.

clips.title: Buried by hand,|or by the *hill*?
clips.yt_title: Was Göbekli Tepe buried on purpose, or did the hillside slide in?
clips.claim: Were Göbekli Tepe's enclosures buried on purpose, or did rubble slide in from the slopes above?
clips.verdict_from: Open too: what the figures meant, whether the enclosures had roofs, and how much of the burying was done by hand.
clips.summary: Rubble moves, so to date Göbekli Tepe the excavators also dated plaster put on its walls while the buildings stood. For about twenty years the story was that people buried the enclosures on purpose. In 2020 the excavators argued most of the fill slid in from the slopes, but at sister site Karahan Tepe, fill capped with big flat stones looks deliberate.

clips.title: How old is|*Puma Punku*?
clips.yt_title: Puma Punku in 15,000 BCE? What radiocarbon and metal cramps say
clips.claim: Was the Puma Punku platform in Bolivia built around fifteen thousand BCE?
clips.verdict_from: Puma Punku in fifteen thousand BCE: ruled out.
clips.summary: High in the Andes of Bolivia, Puma Punku's andesite blocks are cut with crisp inside corners. Arthur Posnansky dated the city to about fifteen thousand BCE from where its walls point at the sky, but radiocarbon from the platform's lowest fill gives about AD 536 to 600, and its metal cramps match Tiwanaku's own era. The tools that cut those corners are still unknown.

clips.title: A *lost world*|behind the giants?
clips.yt_title: Did survivors of a lost Ice Age civilisation teach Göbekli Tepe's builders?
clips.claim: Did survivors of a lost Ice Age civilisation pass their knowledge to Göbekli Tepe's builders?
clips.verdict_from: A lost civilisation behind the giants? A comet strike carved on the Vulture Stone? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out. Just not shown.
clips.summary: The writer Graham Hancock argues that something as ambitious as Göbekli Tepe is no first attempt, and that survivors of a lost Ice Age civilisation may have taught local hunters. Such visitors should leave something with no local roots. So far the dig shows local stone, local tools, homes, cisterns and about a dozen sister sites, but nothing yet from outside.

clips.title: Who really built|*Sacsayhuamán*?
clips.yt_title: Did older builders lay Sacsayhuamán's giant stones before the Incas?
clips.claim: Were the giant lower stones of Sacsayhuamán, above Cusco, laid by builders older than the Incas?
clips.verdict_from: Older builders under Sacsayhuamán: awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: Above Cusco in Peru, Sacsayhuamán's stones of well over a hundred tonnes fit so tightly that a knife blade won't slide between them, and some writers say older builders laid them. Chroniclers writing within a generation describe an Inca work, and Jean-Pierre Protzen came close to the fit with hammerstones. People lived there from about 900 CE, but no older wall has been dated.

clips.chapter: A comet on the Vulture Stone?
clips.title: A comet on the|*Vulture Stone*?
clips.yt_title: Is Göbekli Tepe's Vulture Stone a star map of a comet strike?
clips.claim: Does the Vulture Stone at Göbekli Tepe record a comet strike at the start of the Younger Dryas?
clips.verdict_from: A comet strike carved on the Vulture Stone? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out. Just not shown.
clips.summary: In 2017, the engineer Martin Sweatman read Göbekli Tepe's Vulture Stone as a star map, dated close to a proposed comet strike at the start of the Younger Dryas. The excavators replied that their oldest date for its enclosure is seven hundred to a thousand years younger, and that star matching is flexible. So far, the stars and the stone disagree by centuries.

clips.title: How old are these|*terraces*?
clips.yt_title: Charcoal dates Gunung Padang's stone terraces to about 2,000 years ago
clips.claim: Did people build Gunung Padang's stone terraces about two thousand years ago?
clips.verdict_from: Established: people built these terraces, about two thousand years ago by the charcoal, from columns a volcano made.
clips.summary: Gunung Padang crowns a hill in West Java: five stone terraces, climbing like giant steps. Under the retaining walls, archaeologists found charcoal from fires lit before the walls went up, dating the terraces to about two thousand years ago, built over several generations. Its stone beams came not from a distant quarry but out of the hill itself.

clips.title: A city built|for *hiding*?
clips.yt_title: Derinkuyu: a city cut into soft volcanic rock and built for hiding
clips.claim: Was Derinkuyu, sealed by rolling stone doors, a refuge built for people to hide in?
clips.verdict_from: Underground refuges used by Byzantine Christians in the centuries of the Arab raids: established.
clips.summary: Cappadocia's tuff, a soft stone of volcanic ash, can be cut with hand tools and keeps rooms at a steady temperature. At Derinkuyu, reports count up to eighteen levels, with stables, wine presses, a church and more than fifty air shafts. Stone wheels up to almost two metres across rolled shut from inside, sealing each level on its own: a city built for hiding.

clips.title: Who cut these|*stone beams*?
clips.yt_title: How cooling lava made Gunung Padang's straight-edged stone columns
clips.claim: Were Gunung Padang's straight-edged stone beams shaped by cooling lava, not cut by people?
clips.verdict_from: Established: people built these terraces, about two thousand years ago by the charcoal, from columns a volcano made.
clips.summary: Gunung Padang's long stone beams, five or six sided with edges that look cut, are columnar andesite: lava that shrank and cracked into columns as it cooled, as at the Giant's Causeway. Indonesian volcanologists read the hill as the neck of an ancient volcano, its columns formed right where they lie. Nature made the bricks; the question is who stacked them, and when.

clips.title: One hidden city,|or *hundreds*?
clips.yt_title: Beyond Derinkuyu: Kaymakli, Ozkonak and the city found under Nevsehir
clips.claim: Were Cappadocia's underground cities used as shelters and cellars into the twentieth century?
clips.verdict_from: Their use as shelters and cellars into the twentieth century: established.
clips.summary: Derinkuyu is not alone: Kaymakli lies about ten kilometres north, draining irrigation water revealed Ozkonak in 1972, and surveyors list more than two hundred underground shelters. Under Nevsehir, where families long used the old passages as cellars, finds so far run from about the sixth century to today. Scans there hinted at a city perhaps a third bigger than Derinkuyu.

clips.title: A pyramid from|the *Ice Age*?
clips.yt_title: Is there an Ice Age pyramid inside Gunung Padang? The team's case
clips.claim: Do the scans, cores and soil dates show a pyramid built inside Gunung Padang in the Ice Age?
clips.verdict_from: A pyramid built in the Ice Age? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out. Just not shown.
clips.summary: From 2011, a team led by the geologist Danny Hilman Natawidjaja probed Gunung Padang with radar, electric current and seven drill cores. They read buried layers of columns laid like bricks, a possible chamber where drilling water vanished, and soil dated deep into the Ice Age. If they are right, it is the oldest great building on Earth, by far.

clips.title: Dug to escape|the *Ice Age*?
clips.yt_title: Were Cappadocia's underground cities dug as shelters from the Ice Age?
clips.claim: Were Cappadocia's underground cities first dug as shelters from the cold at the end of the Ice Age?
clips.verdict_from: Shelters from the Ice Age? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out, because the digging itself has never been dated.
clips.summary: The writer Graham Hancock asks whether Cappadocia's underground cities began as shelters from the Ice Age cold of nearly thirteen thousand years ago. He has a point: nobody has ever dated the digging itself, and an empty carved room holds nothing to radiocarbon date. And each enlargement scraped older surfaces away, so the deepest room could be very old, or fairly new.

clips.title: Why was the paper|*retracted*?
clips.yt_title: Why a journal retracted the Gunung Padang Ice Age pyramid paper
clips.claim: Do radiocarbon dates for soil between the stones show an Ice Age pyramid inside Gunung Padang?
clips.verdict_from: A pyramid built in the Ice Age? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out. Just not shown.
clips.summary: The 2023 Gunung Padang pyramid paper dated soil packed between the stones, not charcoal from a hearth, a bone or a tool. Radiocarbon dates when that carbon stopped being alive, not when a stone was laid on top. The journal retracted it in March 2024; the authors say the soil came from built layers, but a date for soil is not a date for a pyramid.

clips.title: Who hid *below*,|and from whom?
clips.yt_title: Who hid in Cappadocia's underground cities? Raids, chapels and refugees
clips.claim: Did Byzantine Christians use Cappadocia's underground cities as refuges from the Arab raids?
clips.verdict_from: Underground refuges used by Byzantine Christians in the centuries of the Arab raids: established.
clips.summary: In Cappadocia's underground cities, what can be dated is what people left: crosses, churches and Byzantine pottery. From the six hundreds the region was a raided Byzantine frontier, and families led their animals below and rolled the stones shut. Most specialists date the great cities to those centuries, but earlier starts, by Phrygians or Hittites, stay open.

clips.title: Did the Ice Age|*come back*?
clips.kicker: Comet and the Cold · Part 1 of 5
clips.yt_title: The Younger Dryas: how Greenland ice and lake mud record the cold's return
clips.claim: Did the north slide back towards Ice Age cold about 12,900 years ago?
clips.verdict_from: The cold snap? Established, in ice and lake mud alike.
clips.summary: About 14,700 years ago, central Greenland warmed by about fourteen degrees, then the north slid back towards Ice Age cold: the Younger Dryas. Yearly bands in Greenland ice put it from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, while mud layers in a German crater lake start it more than a century and a half later. The cold itself is not in doubt; what pulled the trigger is.

clips.title: How old is the|*unreadable* book?
clips.yt_title: The Voynich manuscript's calfskin dates to between about 1404 and 1438
clips.claim: Is the Voynich manuscript a real book from the early 1400s rather than a modern fake?
clips.verdict_from: Established: a real book, on calfskin from the early fourteen hundreds, painted with pigments of its time.
clips.summary: In 1912, the book dealer Wilfrid Voynich bought a batch of old manuscripts near Rome, and inside one lay a letter written in Prague in about 1665. Some suspected Voynich of forging it, but in 2009 radiocarbon dating of its calfskin gave between about 1404 and 1438, and its paints are pigments of the age. Its plants, stars and bathing women still wait for a reader.

clips.title: Did a *comet*|bring the cold?
clips.kicker: Comet and the Cold · Part 2 of 5
clips.yt_title: Did a comet explode over North America 12,900 years ago? The case for it
clips.claim: Did a comet explode over North America about 12,900 years ago and tip the climate into cold?
clips.verdict_from: A comet behind it all? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out, because a burst in the sky can leave only faint traces.
clips.summary: In 2007, a team proposed that a comet exploded over North America about 12,900 years ago and tipped the climate into cold. They reported melted beads, soot and nanodiamonds at the base of a dark layer, the black mat, and Greenland ice shows a platinum spike near the cold's start. One sudden cause would link the cold, the lost giant animals and the end of Clovis tools.

clips.title: Does it count|as a *language*?
clips.yt_title: Does the Voynich text behave like a real language? What the counts show
clips.claim: Do the statistics of the Voynich text point to a real language hidden in its pages?
clips.verdict_from: A real language, enciphered? Or meaningless text, made by hand? Both: Open question.
clips.summary: You can't read the Voynich manuscript, but you can count it. Its words follow the same staircase of frequencies as real languages, crowd by topic like real words, and split into two dialects written by five scribes. Yet its next letter is far easier to guess, matching none of nearly three hundred languages: word by word a language, letter by letter like none we know.

clips.title: Where's the|*crater*?
clips.kicker: Comet and the Cold · Part 3 of 5
clips.yt_title: Are the Carolina Bays craters from a comet blast? Dating the buried sand
clips.claim: Are the Carolina Bays, half a million oval hollows in the eastern United States, a comet's craters?
clips.verdict_from: The Carolina Bays as its craters? Ruled out by the dates.
clips.summary: No crater of the right age has been found for the Younger Dryas comet, though an airburst can leave none. Other teams failed to repeat several clues and found the same markers in black mats of many different ages; the comet team disputes their methods. The Carolina Bays were proposed as its craters, but buried sand dates their rims from 109,000 down to 2,000 years old.

clips.title: Has anyone|*cracked* it?
clips.yt_title: A century of claimed Voynich solutions, and the test every one has failed
clips.claim: Has any claimed solution of the last century actually read the Voynich manuscript?
clips.verdict_from: Already solved, by any reading so far? Ruled out, too.
clips.summary: In 1921 a professor read a hidden message in tiny strokes inside the letters; in 1931 they turned out to be cracks where the ink had dried. Wartime codebreakers under William Friedman never cracked the Voynich manuscript, and readings in Hebrew, Latin and Turkish keep coming. A real reading must follow fixed rules, work on every page, and give a stranger the same text.

clips.title: Did *meltwater*|chill the north?
clips.kicker: Comet and the Cold · Part 4 of 5
clips.yt_title: Did a meltwater flood slow the Atlantic and bring back the cold?
clips.claim: Did a flood of meltwater slow the Atlantic's conveyor belt and trigger the Younger Dryas cold?
clips.verdict_from: What tipped the climate, and what made the platinum? Still open, with meltwater the leading suspect.
clips.summary: Most specialists blame the Younger Dryas cold on meltwater, floating on the Atlantic like a lid and slowing its conveyor of warmth. Arctic seabed cores show a flood down Canada's Mackenzie River that began, within the clocks' margins, just as the cold did. A new reading, still being tested, puts the Greenland platinum spike about forty-five years after the cooling began.

clips.title: Is it beautiful|*nonsense*?
clips.yt_title: Is the Voynich manuscript beautiful nonsense, or a cipher?
clips.claim: Could the Voynich text be meaningless writing, made by hand to look like a language?
clips.verdict_from: A real language, enciphered? Or meaningless text, made by hand? Both: Open question.
clips.summary: In 2004 Gordon Rugg showed that a card with windows, slid over a table of meaningless syllables, makes text very like the Voynich manuscript's. In 2022, volunteers' fake text came out predictable and repetitive too, but so does text from some ciphers, and a 2025 cipher built from dice and playing cards mimics it as well. Nonsense can look like this, and so can a cipher.

clips.title: A comet and the|first *farmers*?
clips.kicker: Comet and the Cold · Part 5 of 5
clips.yt_title: Did a comet blast push Abu Hureyra's villagers into farming?
clips.claim: Did a comet blast melt the glass at Abu Hureyra and push its survivors to take up farming?
clips.verdict_from: A comet behind it all? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out, because a burst in the sky can leave only faint traces.
clips.summary: At Abu Hureyra in Syria, glass the comet team links to a blast is still argued over: another team traced similar droplets to burning mud-brick houses. As the cold set in, the villagers may have begun to cultivate wild rye, some of the first farming on Earth, though others read the seeds differently. The cold mattered either way; who started it is a separate question.

clips.title: Whose *gold* did|Schliemann find?
clips.yt_title: The gold Schliemann named Priam's treasure: about a thousand years too early
clips.claim: Was the gold Schliemann found at Troy in 1873 the treasure of Priam, Troy's king in the Iliad?
clips.verdict_from: Schliemann's gold as Priam's treasure? Ruled out: about a thousand years too early.
clips.summary: In 1868 Frank Calvert showed Heinrich Schliemann a mound called Hisarlik, in northwest Turkey, and from 1871 Schliemann drove a vast trench through it. In 1873 he found gold he named the treasure of Priam, but it came from Troy Two, more than a thousand years older than any date for the war. On the way down, his trench cut away much of the very layers he was looking for.

clips.title: Who were the|*Sea Peoples*?
clips.yt_title: Who were the Sea Peoples? Egypt's temple carvings and the DNA of Ashkelon
clips.claim: Were the Sea Peoples real raiders and migrants who brought destruction?
clips.verdict_from: Raiders and migrants from the sea: real and destructive, established.
clips.summary: Around 1177 BCE, Ramesses the Third carved his battle with invaders from land and sea on his temple, Medinet Habu: the winner's version. Egypt's texts name nine of these peoples, and one, the Peleset, is usually matched with the Philistines. In 2019, DNA from infants at Ashkelon pointed to newcomers, probably from southern Europe: raiders, but also families who stayed.

clips.chapter: The walls and the lower town
clips.title: How *mighty*|was Troy?
clips.yt_title: Walls up to five metres thick: Troy Six and the quarrel over its lower town
clips.claim: Was Troy the seat of power of its region, whatever the size of its lower town?
clips.verdict_from: Established: a strong citadel there, the seat of power of its region.
clips.summary: Wilhelm Doerpfeld uncovered the walls of Troy Six, stone up to five metres thick. From 1988, Manfred Korfmann's team found a ditch and a lower town outside, home to perhaps five to ten thousand people, but the historian Frank Kolb argued Troy was a princely seat, not a real city. Even Kolb called it the centre of its region: the quarrel is over the size of the town.

clips.title: Did one enemy|burn them *all*?
clips.yt_title: Ugarit, Hattusa, Pylos: did one enemy burn the Bronze Age world?
clips.claim: Did one enemy burn the great cities of the Bronze Age, from Greece to Syria?
clips.verdict_from: One culprit for every fire, from Greece to Syria: ruled out.
clips.summary: Ugarit's last king, Ammurapi, wrote that seven enemy ships had done much damage while his troops and ships were far away, and then the city's letters stop. Inland, the Hittite capital, Hattusa, burned, but it had been emptied first, with no sign of raiders from the sea. Greek palaces burned around 1200 BCE, yet on Cyprus, Kition was rebuilt grander than before.

clips.title: A Trojan War in|*Hittite* letters?
clips.yt_title: Wilusa in the Hittite archives: is there a record of the Trojan War?
clips.claim: Do Hittite letters about Wilusa, a name that echoes Homer's Ilios, record a Greek war against it?
clips.verdict_from: Open question. A quarrel over Wilusa is on record. A Greek siege is not.
clips.summary: The archives of Hattusa, the Hittite capital, name a kingdom in the far west, Wilusa, and Homer's Ilios was once Wilios. Around 1250 BCE a Hittite king wrote to the king of Ahhiyawa, most likely the Mycenaean Greeks, that they had been hostile over Wilusa and made peace. Hostile could mean angry letters, or war, and no Hittite text yet found says that Greeks attacked Wilusa.

clips.title: Did the *weather*|turn on them?
clips.yt_title: Tree rings and grain letters: drought and hunger at the end of the Bronze Age
clips.claim: Did drought and hunger strike the Bronze Age kingdoms as they fell?
clips.verdict_from: Drought: strong evidence. Hunger: strong evidence, in their own letters.
clips.summary: Pollen in lake mud from Cyprus, the Syrian coast and the Sea of Galilee shows a long dry spell from around 1200 BCE, and juniper timbers from Gordion record three drought years in a row as the Hittite empire was ending. Letters of the time ask for grain and report severe hunger. Earthquakes are less clear: a 2018 study found a destructive quake at Tiryns and Midea unlikely.

clips.title: How much did|*Homer* remember?
clips.yt_title: A helmet of boars' tusks: how much Bronze Age memory is in the Iliad?
clips.claim: Is the Iliad, composed almost five hundred years after Troy burned, a record of a real war?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: And the war as Homer tells it: Greek kings, ten years, a queen called Helen? Open question.
clips.summary: The Iliad was composed around 700 BCE, almost five hundred years after Troy Seven A burned, but singers recorded in the 1930s show that a tradition without writing can carry old pieces far. It keeps a Bronze Age helmet of boars' tusks, yet its heroes prize iron and the Hittites never appear. It is a chest of heirlooms, some Bronze Age, others added on the way.

clips.title: One cause, or a|*perfect storm*?
clips.yt_title: A perfect storm? The systems collapse idea for the end of the Bronze Age
clips.claim: Did many failures at once, from drought to broken trade and revolt, bring the Bronze Age world down?
clips.verdict_from: And the perfect storm that ties them together: plausible, but hard to test.
clips.summary: Bronze needs copper and tin, almost no kingdom had both, and ships like the one wrecked at Uluburun carried them. Add trouble within, from a Cyprus official blaming Ugarit's own people to a strike by Egypt's tomb builders, and many historians see a systems collapse. But a storm of everything can explain almost anything, and each place fell, or didn't, in its own way.

clips.title: When did *Troy*|really fall?
clips.yt_title: Troy burned around 1180 BCE. Was it Homer's war, or a world coming apart?
clips.claim: Was Troy destroyed around the time Greek tradition places the Trojan War?
clips.verdict_from: A real, rich city on this hill, destroyed around the time Greek tradition places the war? Strong evidence.
clips.summary: Around 1180 BCE, Troy Seven A burned, leaving bronze arrowheads, unburied dead in the streets and heaps of sling stones nobody gathered up. The date later Greek scholars settled on, 1184 BCE, lands right beside the fire. But in the same decades the Hittite capital, Ugarit and Pylos burned too, tree rings record a savage drought, and the ground does not say who lit the fire.

clips.title: How do you fill|a *whole library*?
clips.yt_title: How the Library of Alexandria was filled: books taken from the ships
clips.claim: Was the Ptolemies' library, meant to hold every book worth having, lost in one great fire?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: So, one great fire? Ruled out.
clips.summary: Around 300 BCE, Egypt's Greek kings, the Ptolemies, founded the Mouseion in Alexandria, with a library meant to hold every book worth having. Books on any ship that docked were copied and the library kept the originals, as the third Ptolemy did with Athens' copies of its great playwrights. Callimachus listed its writers in his Tables, now known only from scattered quotations.

clips.title: Could a mind be|*rewritten*?
clips.yt_title: Brain warfare: how the fear of brainwashing led the CIA to MKUltra in 1953
clips.claim: Did MKUltra, born of the fear of brainwashing, ever find a way to control minds?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: Mind control that works: Awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: In 1950 a journalist wrote of brainwashing in communist China, and in the Korean War captured American airmen signed confessions the United States called false. In April 1953 the CIA's head, Allen Dulles, warned of brain warfare, and three days later authorised MKUltra, with LSD as its star. Its records show who was paid, often through fronts, and only roughly why.

clips.title: Did *Caesar* burn|the library?
clips.yt_title: Did Julius Caesar burn the Library of Alexandria in 48 BCE?
clips.claim: Did Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BCE destroy the Library of Alexandria?
clips.verdict_from: Caesar's fire: books burned by the harbour? Strong evidence. The end of the library? Ruled out.
clips.summary: In 48 BCE, trapped in Alexandria, Julius Caesar burned the ships in the harbour. He mentions no books, later writers' figures grow with time, and Cassius Dio says warehouses of grain and books by the docks burned. Yet a generation later Strabo described the Museum at work, and more than a century after the fire Domitian sent scribes to Alexandria to copy its books.

clips.title: Did the CIA drug|*Americans*?
clips.yt_title: MKUltra's safe houses: LSD slipped into the drinks of people who never knew
clips.claim: Did the CIA secretly test LSD on people who did not know they had been drugged?
clips.verdict_from: Did the CIA run illegal drug experiments on people who did not know? Established.
clips.summary: In New York and San Francisco, the CIA paid for safe houses where a narcotics agent, George White, slipped LSD into the drinks of people who had no idea, and some were ill for hours, or days. In 1963, the CIA's own Inspector General warned this put citizens' rights in jeopardy. Gottlieb later guessed about forty tests, and the records that could check him no longer exist.

clips.title: A library lost|without a *fire*?
clips.yt_title: A purge, damp papyrus and war: the slow decline of Alexandria's library
clips.claim: Did the library fade slowly, through a purge of its scholars, decaying papyrus and war?
clips.verdict_from: The purge of 145 BCE? Strong evidence. The palace quarter wrecked in the 270s? Strong evidence.
clips.summary: In 145 BCE, Ptolemy the Eighth turned on Alexandria's scholars, and the head of the library, Aristarchus, fled to Cyprus. Papyrus might last a century, sometimes two or three, so in damp Alexandria a book survived only if someone copied it. In the 270s CE, war wrecked the royal district where the Museum stood, and no writer describes the palace library at work again.

clips.title: How did|*Frank Olson* die?
clips.yt_title: How did Frank Olson die? The scientist given LSD without warning in 1953
clips.claim: How did Frank Olson die, nine days after Gottlieb's team gave him LSD without warning?
clips.verdict_from: And how Frank Olson died is still an Open question.
clips.summary: In November 1953, at a retreat by Deep Creek Lake in Maryland, Gottlieb's team put LSD in a bottle of liqueur, and Frank Olson, a scientist at the Army's Camp Detrick, drank it without warning. Nine days later he fell to his death from a tenth-floor window, recorded as suicide. After his body was exhumed in 1994, the cause was changed to unknown, and two accounts remain.

clips.title: Books to heat|*bathhouses*?
clips.yt_title: Alexandria's books in four thousand bathhouses? The 642 story, checked
clips.claim: Were Alexandria's books burned in 642 to heat four thousand bathhouses for six months?
clips.verdict_from: The caliph's fire? Ruled out.
clips.summary: Alexandria's second library stood in the Serapeum, a temple torn down in 391 CE, yet no account of its fall mentions books. In 415 a mob murdered the philosopher Hypatia, but no ancient source ties her death to the library. The tale that the city's books fed four thousand bathhouses after the 642 conquest first appears in writing about five hundred and sixty years later.

clips.title: What was in the|*seven boxes*?
clips.yt_title: The CIA destroyed the MKUltra files in 1973. Seven boxes of receipts survived
clips.claim: Do the seven boxes that survived tell the whole story of MKUltra?
clips.verdict_from: Do the surviving files tell the whole story? With a hundred and fifty-two files destroyed: Ruled out.
clips.summary: In January 1973 Sidney Gottlieb, with the approval of CIA director Richard Helms, had a hundred and fifty-two MKUltra files destroyed. But the money was filed elsewhere, and in 1977 a CIA employee, seeking files a writer had requested, found seven boxes of vouchers and accounts. Like bank statements after the diaries are burned, they follow the money, not the thinking.

clips.title: Who paid for|*depatterning*?
clips.yt_title: MKUltra in Montreal: the CIA money that helped pay for depatterning
clips.claim: Did the CIA secretly help pay for Ewen Cameron's depatterning of patients in Montreal?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: Did the CIA run illegal drug experiments on people who did not know? Established.
clips.summary: In Montreal, the psychiatrist Ewen Cameron tried to wipe away mental illness with depatterning: weeks of drugged sleep, repeated electroshocks and recorded messages on a loop, and many patients lost years of memory. The CIA helped pay through a front from 1957, though Canada's government gave several times more. In 2025 a Quebec court let former patients bring a class action.

clips.title: Were *Clovis*|hunters first?
clips.yt_title: Clovis first? The spear points that built a wall of dates
clips.claim: Were the Clovis hunters of about thirteen thousand years ago the first people in the Americas?
clips.verdict_from: Clovis first? Ruled out.
clips.summary: In the 1930s, near a railway town in New Mexico, diggers found fluted stone spear points beside mammoth bones, and carbon dating put them at about thirteen thousand years old. A neat story formed: big-game hunters crossed from Asia through Beringia and walked south when the ice parted. Claims of older sites kept failing strict tests, and older dates bounced off the wall.

clips.title: Why is it called|a *dark age*?
clips.yt_title: Britain after Rome: the dark age where the legend puts King Arthur
clips.claim: Was there a real Arthur in the half-lit Britain that Rome left behind?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: And a real war-leader called Arthur? Open question.
clips.summary: Around 410, Rome's last armies left Britain, new Roman coins had stopped arriving in bulk, and almost nobody wrote anything down. Ancient genomes from early medieval graves in eastern England show up to three quarters of the ancestry came from across the North Sea, yet newcomers and Britons lie in the same cemeteries. This half-lit world is where the legend puts Arthur.

clips.title: Who came before|*Clovis*?
clips.yt_title: Older than Clovis: Oregon, Idaho, and a new challenge to Monte Verde
clips.claim: Were people in the Americas before Clovis, more than fourteen thousand years ago?
clips.verdict_from: People here before Clovis, more than fourteen thousand years ago? Established: Oregon and Idaho stand, whatever Monte Verde's age turns out to be.
clips.summary: At Monte Verde in southern Chile, a peat bog sealed a camp with hut frames, mastodon meat and chewed seaweed, about fourteen and a half thousand years old, which experts accepted in 1997. Paisley Caves in Oregon and Cooper's Ferry in Idaho are older than Clovis too. In 2026 a new team argued its dates came from Ice Age wood washed in by the creek, and the jury is out again.

clips.title: Who won the|battle of *Badon*?
clips.yt_title: Gildas, the closest witness to the battle of Badon, never names Arthur
clips.claim: Was there a great British victory over the Saxons at Mount Badon?
clips.verdict_from: A great British victory at Badon? Strong evidence: our one witness was born that year.
clips.summary: Gildas, a British churchman, left the only account of the age by someone who lived through it. He tells of the siege of Mount Badon, a Saxon defeat fought in the year he was born, which points to a real battle within living memory. Yet he never says who led the Britons there, and an old Welsh poem that does name Arthur may have gained that line centuries later.

clips.title: Footprints from|the *Ice Age*?
clips.yt_title: White Sands footprints: seeds, pollen and quartz point to the Ice Age
clips.claim: Do the White Sands footprints show people in the Americas about twenty-one thousand years ago?
clips.verdict_from: People in the Americas by about twenty-one thousand years ago, in the depths of the Ice Age? Strong evidence.
clips.summary: In the bed of a vanished Ice Age lake at White Sands, New Mexico, researchers mapped sixty-one human footprints, mostly of teenagers and children. Seeds of a water plant dated them to about twenty-three to twenty-one thousand years ago, and when critics warned of old carbon in the water, pollen and quartz gave the same answer. Some experts still doubt the dates.

clips.title: When does Arthur|*first* appear?
clips.yt_title: Around 829, a Welsh book calls Arthur a leader of battles, not a king
clips.claim: Was the leader of battles named in the History of the Britons a real man?
clips.verdict_from: And a real war-leader called Arthur? Open question.
clips.summary: The first firm date for Arthur comes around 829, in a Welsh book, the History of the Britons, about three hundred years after the battle of Badon. It calls him a leader of battles, not a king, credits him with nine hundred and sixty men felled in one charge, and already mixes him with folklore. The further we get from Badon, the more we learn about Arthur.

clips.title: A *kelp highway*|to the Americas?
clips.yt_title: Down the coast or through the ice? How the first Americans may have come
clips.claim: Did the first Americans come down the coast, rather than through the ice-free corridor?
clips.verdict_from: And the road? Down the coast first: Plausible.
clips.summary: Twenty-two thousand years ago, ice covered almost all of Canada, yet the White Sands walkers were already south of it. The inland gap didn't fully reopen until about thirteen thousand eight hundred years ago, but islands off Alaska were ice-free by about seventeen thousand years ago, with food-rich kelp forests along the coast. Any camps on that old shore now lie underwater.

clips.title: Did monks find|*Arthur's* grave?
clips.yt_title: Did Glastonbury Abbey's monks really find King Arthur's grave?
clips.claim: Did the monks of Glastonbury Abbey find the grave of King Arthur?
clips.verdict_from: His grave at Glastonbury? Ruled out: its cross speaks the language of a legend six centuries younger.
clips.summary: Around 1136, Geoffrey of Monmouth made Arthur a king, conceived at Tintagel and carried away to Avalon, in a medieval bestseller. Seven years after fire destroyed Glastonbury Abbey, its monks announced they had found Arthur, with a cross whose words echo Geoffrey's story, not the 500s. Most historians see the find as a publicity stunt, made just when the abbey needed it most.

clips.title: What does|ancient *DNA* say?
clips.yt_title: Ancient DNA and the first Americans: do the genes fit the footprints?
clips.claim: Were people in the Americas by twenty-one thousand years ago, as early as the genes' first parting?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: People in the Americas by about twenty-one thousand years ago, in the depths of the Ice Age? Strong evidence.
clips.summary: Ancient genomes suggest the ancestors of Native Americans paused in Beringia, cut off by the ice, until their branches parted around twenty thousand years ago. Yet the White Sands footprints are as old as that parting, or older. Either the genetic clocks need adjusting, or the first walkers left few or no descendants, or, say the sceptics, the footprint dates are wrong.

clips.title: Can we dig up|*Camelot*?
clips.yt_title: Was Cadbury Castle really Camelot? What the digs there and at Tintagel found
clips.claim: Was Cadbury Castle Camelot, or Tintagel the place where Arthur was born?
clips.verdict_from: Camelot at Cadbury, or Arthur's birth at Tintagel? Awaiting evidence: the right places, the right century, and no name.
clips.summary: From around 470, someone powerful refortified Cadbury Castle, a Somerset hill that locals called Camelot by 1542, and raised a great timber hall there. Tintagel has given more Mediterranean pottery than any other site in Britain, and a slate scratched with a different name, Artognou. Powerful people lived in both places, but none of them left us the name Arthur.

clips.title: Can we trust|the *sagas*?
clips.yt_title: Leif Eriksson and Vinland: what the two sagas say, and where they disagree
clips.claim: Did Norse voyagers reach a land west of Greenland, as the sagas tell?
clips.verdict_from: The Norse in America, around the year one thousand? Established.
clips.summary: Around the year one thousand, the sagas say, Leif Eriksson sailed west from Greenland to a land they call Vinland, where Norse settlers traded with its people, then fought them. But the sagas were written down about two centuries later, and they disagree on the details. For nine centuries, the story was all there was: no one had found a single Norse house beyond Greenland.

clips.title: How old is the|*Minotaur* myth?
clips.yt_title: Homer knew King Minos of Knossos, but never mentioned the Minotaur
clips.claim: Does the Greek myth of Minos remember a real palace, a bull cult and a sea power?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: So does the myth remember a real palace, a bull cult and a sea power? Plausible.
clips.summary: In the Greek myth, King Minos kept the Minotaur, half man, half bull, in a maze built by Daedalus, until Theseus killed it and followed Ariadne's thread back out. Yet Homer knows Minos of Knossos and never mentions a maze or a monster, and our fullest tellings come more than fourteen centuries after the palace's last great fire. Does the story remember anything real?

clips.title: A Viking camp|in *Newfoundland*?
clips.yt_title: Under the turf at L'Anse aux Meadows: a Norse base in Newfoundland
clips.claim: Are the ruins at L'Anse aux Meadows, in Newfoundland, a Norse site?
clips.verdict_from: The Norse in America, around the year one thousand? Established.
clips.summary: In 1960, a local man led the explorer Helge Ingstad to grassy bumps at L'Anse aux Meadows, in Newfoundland. Eight years of digs, led by the archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad, uncovered eight sod buildings, a bronze cloak pin, a smithy and broken iron nails from ship repairs. No shelters for animals: not a farm, but a base for mending ships and exploring.

clips.title: A palace built|like a *maze*?
clips.yt_title: Knossos: the palace Arthur Evans found, and the parts he rebuilt in concrete
clips.claim: Did a great palace stand at Knossos, right where the myth puts King Minos?
clips.verdict_from: Established: a great palace of hundreds of rooms, right where the myth puts Minos.
clips.summary: In 1900, Arthur Evans began digging at Knossos, on Crete, and within months uncovered a maze of corridors, staircases, light wells and storerooms around a central court. He believed he had found the palace of Minos. But much of what visitors see is his reconstruction in reinforced concrete, which critics say set his guesses in stone and admirers say made the ruins readable.

clips.chapter: A storm in the tree rings
clips.title: How do we know|the year was *1021*?
clips.yt_title: How a radiocarbon spike in tree rings dated the Norse in Newfoundland to 1021
clips.claim: Were the Norse cutting trees in Newfoundland in the year 1021?
clips.verdict_from: The Norse in America, around the year one thousand? Established.
clips.summary: Radiocarbon gives only a rough date, but in 993 a burst of particles, most likely from the Sun, left extra radiocarbon in that year's ring in every growing tree. Three pieces of Norse wood from L'Anse aux Meadows, cut with metal blades, show that spike twenty-eight rings from the bark: 1021. The researchers call it the first known moment when humans had circled the globe.

clips.title: Why so many|*bulls* at Knossos?
clips.yt_title: Bulls and double axes at Knossos: clues to the myth, or only ideas?
clips.claim: Were bulls at the heart of the art and ritual of Knossos?
clips.verdict_from: Established: bulls at the heart of its art and ritual.
clips.summary: At Knossos, bulls are everywhere: a painting of young people vaulting a charging bull, stone vessels carved as bulls' heads, stone horns on the rooftops. Whether such rituals grew into a tale of a deadly bull is only a thought, and many linguists doubt the link between labyrinth and the double axe. Whatever the myth made of it, the bull sits at the heart of the palace's art.

clips.title: Where was the land|of *grapes*?
clips.yt_title: Where was Vinland? The butternuts that point to journeys south
clips.claim: Where exactly was Vinland, and how long did the Norse stay?
clips.verdict_from: How long they stayed, and where exactly Vinland was? Open question.
clips.summary: Among the wood chips at the Norse camp in Newfoundland lay three butternuts and butternut wood cut with a metal knife. Butternuts don't grow there: the nearest grow almost nine hundred kilometres away, in New Brunswick, on shores where wild grapes grow too. So was Vinland a whole region around the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, and did the Norse stay for years or a century?

clips.title: Honey for the|*Labyrinth*?
clips.yt_title: Honey for the Mistress of the Labyrinth: what Linear B reveals at Knossos
clips.claim: Does a clay tablet from Knossos record the word labyrinth?
clips.verdict_from: Strong evidence: the word labyrinth in the palace's own records, on the usual reading.
clips.summary: Crete's Linear A is still unread, but in 1952 Michael Ventris, building on Alice Kober's work, cracked Linear B: Greek, used for the palace's accounts at Knossos. One list, on the usual reading, sends honey to all the gods and the same again to the Mistress of the Labyrinth. So the word was written at Knossos centuries before Homer; what it named, the tablet doesn't say.

clips.title: Which Viking finds|*don't* hold up?
clips.yt_title: The Vinland Map and the Kensington Runestone: why both are ruled out
clips.claim: Are the Vinland Map and the Kensington Runestone as old as they were said to be?
clips.verdict_from: The Vinland Map? Ruled out: a modern ink. The Kensington Runestone? Ruled out: a modern language.
clips.summary: In 1965, Yale unveiled a map said to be from the fifteenth century, with Vinland on it, but its ink holds a titanium pigment first made in the 1920s. The Kensington Runestone, reported tangled in tree roots, tells of Swedes and Norwegians in 1362, yet its language reads like Swedish of the 1800s. A possible Norse site at Point Rosee, dug again, showed no Norse presence.

clips.title: Did a volcano|end *Knossos*?
clips.yt_title: The Thera eruption and the long end of the palace of Knossos
clips.claim: Did a real memory of the palace of Knossos survive into the Greek myth?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: So does the myth remember a real palace, a bull cult and a sea power? Plausible.
clips.summary: A little over a hundred kilometres north of Crete, the volcano of Thera exploded in one of the largest eruptions in human history. Yet Knossos carried on for generations, through fires and Greek-speaking masters, to a last great fire whose date is still debated. Long after, the Greek city of Knossos stamped a labyrinth on its coins: how far had the memory travelled?

clips.title: Why did spies|fund *psychics*?
clips.yt_title: The psychic arms race, and the crane drawing two analysts called accurate
clips.claim: Did two analysts really call Pat Price's crane drawing accurate?
clips.verdict_from: So is the crane: two analysts really did call it accurate.
clips.summary: In 1972, an Army report warned that Soviet psychic research could be ahead, and American intelligence soon funded tests at the Stanford Research Institute. In 1974, given only map coordinates, Pat Price drew a crane that two analysts called accurate. But the officer in charge wrote that most of Price's data were wrong or unverifiable: the crane is what everyone remembers.

clips.title: Who was|*Piri Reis*?
clips.kicker: The Piri Reis Map · Part 1 of 5
clips.yt_title: Piri Reis: the Ottoman sailor behind the famous map, and his Book of the Sea
clips.claim: Did the Ottoman sailor Piri Reis draw the world map that bears his name, in 1513?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: Established: Piri Reis drew this map in 1513, from about twenty sources, and he told us so.
clips.summary: Piri Reis was born around 1470 and sailed with his uncle, the corsair Kemal Reis, fighting Venetian fleets for the sultan. His Book of the Sea guided sailors round the whole Mediterranean, coast by coast, marking harbours, fresh water and hidden rocks, and more than forty copies survive. Yet his first great work, begun around 1511, was a map of the whole world.

clips.title: Did the Army run|*psychic* spies?
clips.yt_title: The Army's psychic spy unit at Fort Meade, from Gondola Wish to Star Gate
clips.claim: Did the Army really run a psychic spy unit at Fort Meade?
clips.verdict_from: The programme itself: Established. Twenty-three years, about twenty million dollars, in the government's own files.
clips.summary: From 1977, the Army ran a small psychic spy unit at Fort Meade, in Maryland, where viewers given only coordinates or a code sketched whatever came to mind. Insiders tell of striking hits, but those stories are hard to check. From the first dollars to the end, the programme ran twenty-three years and cost about twenty million dollars.

clips.title: A lost chart by|*Columbus*?
clips.kicker: The Piri Reis Map · Part 2 of 5
clips.yt_title: Inside the Piri Reis map: about twenty sources and a lost chart by Columbus
clips.claim: Does the Caribbean on the Piri Reis map come from a lost chart by Columbus?
clips.verdict_from: Strong evidence: his notes say so, and the map carries Columbus's ideas and his place names.
clips.summary: Piri Reis finished his world map in 1513, on gazelle skin; the surviving third turned up in 1929 at Topkapi Palace. His notes list about twenty sources, among them a map by Columbus, and the map carries Columbus's ideas: a huge Hispaniola, and Cuba drawn as a coast. Columbus's own chart is lost, so this map holds the only known copy of it, in part.

clips.title: How do you test|a *psychic*?
clips.yt_title: Remote viewing in the lab: beating chance, or clues in the transcripts?
clips.claim: Did the remote viewing lab tests show a real psychic effect?
clips.verdict_from: A psychic effect in the lab? Awaiting evidence. The scores are on paper; what caused them was never pinned down.
clips.summary: At the Stanford Research Institute, judges ranked which site each viewer's description fitted best, and star viewers beat chance by a wide margin. Psychologists David Marks and Richard Kammann could not repeat it, and found clues in the transcripts, such as dates; the lab said its hits still beat chance without them. What caused the scores was never pinned down.

clips.title: Antarctica, drawn|before the *ice*?
clips.kicker: The Piri Reis Map · Part 3 of 5
clips.yt_title: How the claim of an ice-free Antarctica on the Piri Reis map began
clips.claim: Does the Piri Reis map show the coast of Antarctica as it was before the ice?
clips.verdict_from: And Antarctica, drawn before the ice? Ruled out.
clips.summary: In 1956, navigator Arlington Mallery suggested the bottom coast of the Piri Reis map was Antarctica before the ice; a 1960 Air Force letter said it matched the rock beneath the ice remarkably well. Charles Hapgood saw Ice Age seafarers behind it. On his own reading, the map leaves out about fourteen hundred kilometres of coast and the Drake Passage: copying slips, he argued.

clips.title: Was psychic spying|ever *useful*?
clips.yt_title: The 1995 review of psychic spying: did remote viewing ever guide an operation?
clips.claim: Did remote viewing ever produce reliable intelligence?
clips.verdict_from: Did remote viewing produce reliable intelligence? Ruled out, by the programme's own evaluation.
clips.summary: In 1995, an outside review found a statistically significant effect in the lab, though its two experts, one convinced and one a sceptic, disagreed on what it meant. In the field, reports were vague and ambiguous, and had never guided an intelligence operation. The unit was shut down, though its defenders said the review judged only its final operations.

clips.title: Why does the|coast *bend*?
clips.kicker: The Piri Reis Map · Part 4 of 5
clips.yt_title: Why does the southern coast of the Piri Reis map bend? Three clues
clips.claim: What was the bending southern coast of the Piri Reis map drawn from?
clips.verdict_from: What exactly the southern coast was drawn from: a report, a guess, or a fashion of the age? Open question.
clips.summary: The southern coast of the Piri Reis map runs straight on from South America, with no Drake Passage. Piri's hide curves at one corner, he had only guesses and reports beyond a point in Brazil, and his age imagined a great southern land; his note reports a barren land, full of great snakes and very hot. So was it drawn from a report, a guess, or a fashion of the age?

clips.title: How old is the|ice in *Antarctica*?
clips.kicker: The Piri Reis Map · Part 5 of 5
clips.yt_title: When was Queen Maud Land last free of ice? Millions of years ago, not thousands
clips.claim: Could Antarctica's coast have been free of ice recently enough for anyone to map it?
clips.verdict_from: And Antarctica, drawn before the ice? Ruled out.
clips.summary: When two Russian ships came within twenty miles of Queen Maud Land in January 1820, the first part of Antarctica anyone is known to have seen, what they saw was ice. An ice core from its heart runs unbroken back a hundred and fifty thousand years. And sea-floor mud says Antarctica has carried ice sheets for about thirty-four million years.

clips.title: Flying disc, or|*foil and sticks*?
clips.yt_title: The Roswell base announced a flying disc. The photos show foil and sticks
clips.claim: Was the flying disc the Roswell base announced in July 1947 an alien craft?
clips.verdict_from: Every document from that July describes rubber, foil, paper and sticks, and nothing from the time describes anything else. Ruled out.
clips.summary: In June 1947 a ranch foreman north-west of Roswell found scattered rubber, tinfoil, paper and sticks. On the eighth of July the air base announced it had a flying disc; that evening a general showed reporters the debris, which his weather officer named a balloon with a radar target. From about two kilos of debris grew the world's most famous flying saucer story.

clips.title: Built from blocks,|or *carved*?
clips.kicker: Age of the Sphinx · Part 1 of 5
clips.yt_title: Carved, not built: the rock layers that tie the Sphinx to its temple
clips.claim: Was the Sphinx carved from the bedrock, with its quarried stone used to build the temple in front?
clips.verdict_from: Carved from the living rock, its quarry feeding the temple in front: established.
clips.summary: The Great Sphinx was carved, not stacked: a U-shaped trench was cut around a block of layered bedrock at Giza, and the stone dug out built a temple in front. In 1980 the geologist Thomas Aigner found that most of the temple's 173 big blocks carry the same yellow band that crosses the lion's chest. The Sphinx is what the quarrymen left standing.

clips.title: A second crash,|with *bodies*?
clips.yt_title: Roswell, thirty years on: how the story grew to two saucers and eight aliens
clips.claim: Was there a second crash site with bodies, as accounts given decades later said?
clips.verdict_from: Bodies, or a second craft hidden elsewhere? Awaiting evidence, after almost eighty years.
clips.summary: In 1978 a researcher tracked down Jesse Marcel, long retired, who said the Roswell weather balloon had been a cover story. Books followed and the story grew: a second crash site with bodies, then two saucers and eight aliens, in versions that disagree on where it fell and who was aboard. Most were told thirty to fifty years on, and memories drift without anyone lying.

clips.title: Who left *tools*|in the trench?
clips.kicker: Age of the Sphinx · Part 2 of 5
clips.yt_title: Khafre's causeway, a jar and copper-flecked hammers: dating the Sphinx
clips.claim: Was the Sphinx carved as part of Khafre's building works, around 2500 BCE?
clips.verdict_from: Carved in Khafre's building works, around 2500 BCE: strong evidence. Khufu or Djedefre would shift that by decades.
clips.summary: The Sphinx lies at the foot of the causeway to Khafre's pyramid at Giza, and its trench's south wall is the causeway's edge, so the trench came later. In 1978 a corner of the trench gave up abandoned blocks, half a pyramid-age jar and stone hammers, one flecked with copper. Most Egyptologists credit Khafre; his father or brother would move the date by decades, not millennia.

clips.title: Did a *secret*|fall on the ranch?
clips.yt_title: Project Mogul: the secret balloon train that matches the Roswell debris
clips.claim: Was the Roswell debris from a secret Project Mogul balloon train?
clips.verdict_from: The debris, from a Mogul balloon train: Strong evidence. It matches down to the tape; the gap is which flight, exactly.
clips.summary: In 1994 the Air Force named a 1947 secret: Project Mogul, trains of balloons carrying microphones to listen for Soviet atomic tests. Their radar reflectors were balsa sticks and foil-backed paper, made by a toy company that used its own tape printed with flowers, a match for the debris on the Roswell ranch. Which train came down there is still argued.

clips.title: Carved before|the *pharaohs*?
clips.kicker: Age of the Sphinx · Part 3 of 5
clips.yt_title: The rain case for an older Sphinx: Robert Schoch's reading of the walls
clips.claim: Does the weathering in the Sphinx's pit show it was carved thousands of years before the pharaohs?
clips.verdict_from: A Sphinx carved thousands of years before the pharaohs? Awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: Around 1990 the geologist Robert Schoch read the Sphinx's deeply worn walls as rain at work for thousands of years, and sound waves sent into the floor found weathering deeper in front than behind. He put the first carving thousands of years before the pharaohs, later about twelve thousand years ago. For him the walls are a clock; the question is whether it keeps good time.

clips.chapter: Dummies, a film and lost files
clips.title: Alien bodies,|or test *dummies*?
clips.yt_title: Sixty-seven test dummies: the Air Force's answer to the Roswell bodies
clips.claim: Were the bodies people recalled at Roswell test dummies and later accidents, merged in memory?
clips.verdict_from: The bodies, as later memories merged: Plausible.
clips.summary: In 1995 auditors found only two documents from 1947 about Roswell, and the base's outgoing messages had been destroyed. The man who released a famous autopsy film admitted it was a re-creation, and in 1997 the Air Force's answer for the bodies was test dummies and later accidents, merged in memory. To many people it sounded like one more change, and trust ran out.

clips.title: Worn by rain,|or by *salt*?
clips.kicker: Age of the Sphinx · Part 4 of 5
clips.yt_title: Salt, damp sand and fast decay: the other reading of the Sphinx's worn walls
clips.claim: Beyond the worn walls, does anything point to a Sphinx carved thousands of years before the pharaohs?
clips.verdict_from: Awaiting evidence. Its case rests on one reading of the weathering, which salt, damp sand and fast decay can also explain.
clips.summary: Other geologists found salt in the Sphinx's soft layers, where growing crystals burst the grains into rounded hollows with no rain needed, and damp sand in the pit ate at the rock for centuries. Four stones of its temple, dated by when they last saw sunlight, came out between about 3100 and 1200 BCE, and nobody has found a workplace at Giza from before Egypt's first farmers.

clips.title: What lies *under*|the Sphinx?
clips.kicker: Age of the Sphinx · Part 5 of 5
clips.yt_title: What lies under the Sphinx? Radar, drill holes and a hollow picked up in 1991
clips.claim: Is there anything under the Sphinx besides natural rock and cracks?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: A Sphinx carved thousands of years before the pharaohs? Awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: Around 1400 BCE the king Thutmose the Fourth cleared the Sphinx's sand, gave its body a new skin of limestone and set a granite slab telling his dream between its paws. Since 1978 teams have scanned beneath it with radar and sound, and where drills went down, cameras found only natural rock and cracks. Whether any crossed the hollow picked up in 1991, no report says.

clips.title: Burnt logs, or|*books*?
clips.yt_title: Herculaneum, 1752: the charred lumps that turned out to be books
clips.claim: Were the black lumps found in a buried villa at Herculaneum books turned to charcoal?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: Can we read ancient books that would crumble if anyone opened them? Established.
clips.summary: In 1750 well diggers on the Bay of Naples hit a Roman villa buried by Vesuvius. From 1752 it gave up hundreds of black lumps, taken for burnt logs until one broke open with writing inside: rolls of papyrus turned to charcoal, so brittle a touch made them ash. The favourite candidate for the library's owner, Julius Caesar's father-in-law, is a good guess, not yet a fact.

clips.title: Giant steps|*under the sea*?
clips.yt_title: The giant steps a diver found off Yonaguni in 1986, and named Ruins Point
clips.claim: Is the giant underwater staircase off Yonaguni a monument made by people?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: A monument carved by people? Awaiting evidence.
clips.summary: In 1986 a diver off Yonaguni, the last island at Japan's western end, saw the sea floor turn into giant stairs and named the spot Ruins Point. The marine geologist Masaaki Kimura mapped its flat terraces and sheer walls, about two hundred and seventy metres long and twenty-five high. To many divers it looks built; other geologists answer that it is the rock and the sea.

clips.title: How do you open|a *charcoal* book?
clips.yt_title: A year for half a roll: Piaggio's machine and the Herculaneum scrolls
clips.claim: Can rolls of papyrus turned to charcoal be opened and read at all?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: Can we read ancient books that would crumble if anyone opened them? Established.
clips.summary: Early attempts on the charred Herculaneum rolls sliced some in half, copying each layer by hand and scraping it away: to read a page, you destroyed it. From 1753 Antonio Piaggio's machine eased layers free on gummed threads, and the first roll out of it was by Philodemus, a philosopher arguing that music cannot change your character. Hundreds of rolls were never opened at all.

clips.title: A gate, a road,|a *stone face*?
clips.yt_title: Masaaki Kimura's case for a carved monument under the sea at Yonaguni
clips.claim: Is the Yonaguni formation a monument carved by people, as Masaaki Kimura argues?
clips.verdict_from: A monument carved by people? Awaiting evidence. Not ruled out, because nobody has dug.
clips.summary: The marine geologist Masaaki Kimura read the formation off Yonaguni like a ruin: a ring road, retaining walls, a gate with paving stones, a drainage channel and dents he took for wedge marks. His team reported a slab with incised lines and a round stone carved with an animal. It is all one piece of bedrock, but people have carved whole temples out of living rock.

clips.title: Can X-rays|*unroll* a scroll?
clips.yt_title: Black ink on a black page: reading a charred scroll without opening it
clips.claim: Can X-rays read a charred scroll without anyone opening it?
clips.verdict_from: Can we read ancient books that would crumble if anyone opened them? Established.
clips.summary: The computer scientist Brent Seales bet on never opening the scrolls: X-ray each one slice by slice, follow one sheet through, and flatten it on screen. In 2015 it worked on a charred scroll from En-Gedi, whose ink held traces of metal, but Herculaneum's ink is mostly soot, black on a black page. Next came brighter X-rays, and a computer trained to see it.

clips.title: Can rock break|into *stairs*?
clips.yt_title: Flat layers and straight cracks: how Yonaguni's rock makes its own stairs
clips.claim: Are the Yonaguni steps the natural way this island's layered sandstone and mudstone break?
clips.verdict_from: Established: this is the island's own bedrock, layered sandstone and mudstone that splits into flat steps and right angles
clips.summary: Yonaguni's sandstone and mudstone split along flat layers and crack straight down in sets that often cross at right angles, and waves pry out the blocks between. On the island's south-east coast, the same rock steps down to the sea in the open air. The geologist Robert Schoch came hoping for a monument and judged it primarily natural, though people may have touched up parts.

clips.title: What *word* hid|in the scroll?
clips.yt_title: Porphyras, purple: the first word read inside a closed Herculaneum scroll
clips.claim: Can a computer pick out words inside a closed scroll that no one can unroll?
clips.verdict_from: Established. Independent teams found the same letters, specialists read them, and the newest scans show the ink itself.
clips.summary: In 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge put scans of the Herculaneum scrolls online, with prizes for reading them. A student trained a model on a faint crackle of ink spotted by a contestant, and the first word read inside a closed scroll appeared: porphyras, purple, also found there with a different method. The 2024 grand prize was for about five per cent of one scroll.

clips.title: Stalactites|*below the waves*?
clips.yt_title: Stalactites under the sea: when Yonaguni's steps were last dry land
clips.claim: Did the Yonaguni rock stand in open air through the Ice Age, until the sea closed over it?
clips.verdict_from: Established too: it stood in the open air through the Ice Age, and the sea closed over it
clips.summary: In the last Ice Age the sea stood far lower: a drowned cave off Yonaguni, seventeen metres down, holds stalactites, some tens of thousands of years old, and they only grow in air. Sea-level curves put the rising water at the rock's foot roughly nine to ten thousand years ago, over its upper steps by about seven thousand. If people carved it, they did it while it was dry.

clips.title: A whole scroll,|read *end to end*?
clips.yt_title: What is left of a Herculaneum scroll, read end to end for the first time
clips.claim: Has what survives of a Herculaneum scroll been read from end to end?
clips.verdict_from: A whole scroll, read end to end? Strong evidence, for what survives of it.
clips.summary: In 2026 came the first complete reading of a charred Herculaneum scroll, one written off as unreadable after attempts to open it stripped its outer layers. Its core gave up thirty-one turns and twenty-two columns of Greek: Stoic ethics, already an antique when Vesuvius buried it. Some scrolls are crushed so tight that their layers blur, and success is not guaranteed.

clips.title: Carved by hand,|or by *the sea*?
clips.yt_title: Did anyone shape Yonaguni's steps? The traces a quarry would leave behind
clips.claim: Did anyone ever shape the Yonaguni steps, leaving the traces a quarry would?
clips.verdict_from: Open: whether anyone ever shaped it.
clips.summary: People reached these islands at least thirty thousand years ago, and in 2019 paddlers crossed from Taiwan in a dugout canoe. A quarry leaves rows of wedge slots, chips, broken tools and hearths. As far as we know, the carved finds reported there lack a published find spot, layer and date, and no controlled dig in the mud on the drowned terraces has ever been published.

clips.title: What was inside|the *bronze lump*?
clips.yt_title: Sponge divers, a wreck full of statues and a bronze lump with a gear inside
clips.claim: Was the corroded lump raised from the Antikythera wreck a Greek calculator of the sky?
clips.verdict_from: Sets up: A Greek calculator of the sky, with gears for the Sun, the Moon, eclipses, calendars and games? Established
clips.summary: In 1900 sponge divers sheltering from a storm off the small island of Antikythera found a wreck heaped with bronze and marble statues. Among the lumps of corroded bronze and wood raised with them, one split open as it dried in 1902: inside were a gear wheel and tiny Greek letters. For half a century, nobody could say for sure what kind of machine it was.

clips.title: Why *127 teeth*|on one wheel?
clips.yt_title: Counting 127 teeth: how X-rays tied the Antikythera gears to the Moon
clips.claim: Were the Antikythera gears cut to follow the Moon's cycles across the sky?
clips.verdict_from: A Greek calculator of the sky, with gears for the Sun, the Moon, eclipses, calendars and games? Established
clips.summary: The historian of science Derek de Solla Price called the Antikythera fragments an ancient Greek computer, and in 1971 he X-rayed them and counted the teeth. One wheel had 127: doubled, 254, the number of times the Moon goes round the sky in nineteen years. Sharper pictures later fixed his mistakes, and each new way of seeing found more gears.

clips.title: The sky in|a *shoebox*?
clips.yt_title: Eclipses, a calendar and the Olympics: what the Antikythera gears tracked
clips.claim: Was the Antikythera mechanism a calculator of the sky, with gears for eclipses, calendars and games?
clips.verdict_from: Established: the gears, the dials and the words are in the bronze.
clips.summary: In 2005 an eight-tonne X-ray scanner was brought to the Antikythera fragments in Athens. Turned by hand, the gears drive pointers for the Sun, the Moon and the date, a pin in a slot copying the Moon's uneven pace, while back dials count a nineteen-year calendar, an eclipse cycle and the games. It is the sky as the Greeks read it, in a box about the size of a shoebox.

clips.title: Did it track|the *planets*?
